# References and further reading

This book quotes no one, so this page is not a bibliography. It is a way out: where to read further
on topics the book only introduces. Official Nim documentation comes first because it follows the
language version, while this book follows its own release. Every link was checked alive in October
2026.

## Official Nim documentation

- **[Nim Manual](https://nim-lang.org/docs/manual.html)** — the full language rules: `type`, `effect`,
  `{.pragma.}`, and the details this book compresses.
- **[Standard Library](https://nim-lang.org/docs/lib.html)** — every bundled module; start here when
  something is missing from chapter 28.
- **[Tutorial part 1](https://nim-lang.org/docs/tut1.html)** and
  **[part 2](https://nim-lang.org/docs/tut2.html)** — a fast path for readers who already write code
  in another language.
- **[Compiler User Guide](https://nim-lang.org/docs/nimc.html)** — every `nim c` flag, including
  `-d:release`, `--mm`, and `--filenames` from chapters 1 and 33.
- **[NEP-1: Nim style guide](https://nim-lang.org/docs/nep1.html)** — the naming rules behind chapter 3.
- **[Nim tools](https://nim-lang.org/docs/tools.html)** — `nimpretty`, `nimble`, and the rest of what
  sits around the compiler.
- **[Nimble](https://nim-lang.github.io/nimble/)** — documentation for the package manager used in
  chapter 37.

## Memory and ownership

- **[Memory management](https://nim-lang.org/docs/mm.html)** — ARC, ORC, and the `--mm` choices; the
  long version of chapter 27.
- **[Destructors and move semantics](https://nim-lang.org/docs/destructors.html)** — `=destroy`,
  `=copy`, `=sink`, and `move`.
- **[Introduction to ARC/ORC in Nim](https://nim-lang.org/blog/2020/10/15/introduction-to-arc-orc-in-nim.html)**
  — background that explains the design reasoning, not just the rules.
- **[Introducing ORC](https://nim-lang.org/blog/2020/12/08/introducing-orc.html)** — the cycle
  collector, written by the compiler's author.
- **[Nim 2.0 released](https://nim-lang.org/blog/2023/08/01/nim-v20-released.html)** — why ORC became
  the default memory manager.

## Async, HTTP, and threads

- **[std/asyncdispatch](https://nim-lang.org/docs/asyncdispatch.html)** — `async`, `await`, and
  `Future`; the basis of chapter 31.
- **[std/asynchttpserver](https://nim-lang.org/docs/asynchttpserver.html)** — the HTTP server used in
  chapter 35.
- **[std/httpclient](https://nim-lang.org/docs/httpclient.html)** — the client side of the same chapter.
- **[std/typedthreads](https://nim-lang.org/docs/typedthreads.html)** — typed threads, chapter 42.

## Backends, FFI, and data

- **[Backend integration](https://nim-lang.org/docs/backends.html)** — what to prepare when calling C,
  the long version of chapter 32.
- **[std/db_common](https://nim-lang.org/docs/db_common.html)** — the interface behind `db_sqlite` in
  chapter 36.
- **[std/json](https://nim-lang.org/docs/json.html)** — parsing and serialising, used in chapter 28.

## Books and examples

- **[Nim in Action](https://www.manning.com/books/nim-in-action)** — Dominik Picheta, Manning, 2017.
  The most complete printed book on Nim; some examples predate the current language, so compare with
  the manual.
- **[nim-in-action-code](https://github.com/dom96/nim-in-action-code)** — the example code for that book.

## When a link dies

Almost every address above lives on `nim-lang.org` and `github.com`, the two most stable names in this
ecosystem. If one of them moves, search the title on the
[official documentation](https://nim-lang.org/documentation.html) page, which is the main index.
